record.venue: International Journal of Public Sector Management
record.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how controllers in public healthcare envision human–AI collaboration in management control when dealing with uncertainty, complexity and equivocality, focusing on anticipated advantages and implementation challenges in an early-adoption setting. Design/methodology/approach We conducted an exploratory qualitative study with 14 controllers from Italian public healthcare organisations. Four closed-ended questions provided a preliminary picture of current AI adoption, while three scenario-based open-ended questions elicited prospective assessments. The framework method was used to analyse the data. Findings AI adoption remains limited and uneven, and is rarely embedded in everyday management control. Under uncertainty, controllers link AI to better forecasting and faster access to information, but worry about data quality, privacy and overreliance. In complex settings, they expect AI to help integrate diverse information and enable more systemic control, provided processes are standardised and human oversight remains. In equivocal situations, AI may support interpretation and communication, but its impact is limited by limited hands-on experience and the difficulty of codifying contextual nuances. Originality/value Based on the Jarrahi (2018) decision-making scenarios, the study develops a tentative conceptualisation of how public healthcare controllers envisage AI collaboration. The concerns of the participants inform three proposed arrangements: validation, recursive integration and contestable sensemaking. Their formulation and the accountability-augmentation principle are theoretical elaborations informed by prospective evidence and accountability research.

record.abstract_text: Purpose Agentic AI systems execute procurement decisions, reroute shipments and renegotiate supplier contracts at speeds that preclude real-time human review. The existing literature offers limited analytical attention to the risks that arise when decision authority is delegated to agents. This paper develops a risk taxonomy for agentic AI in supply chains and traces the hierarchical dependencies and influence magnitudes among the identified risks. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of literature, analyzed through theories–characteristics–contexts–methods framework, produces the risk taxonomy. A hybrid modified total interpretive structural modeling and fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory methodology is then applied to structured expert judgments to establish the causal hierarchy and quantify inter-risk influence. Findings Three risks, namely workforce skill gap, data quality and reliability and ethical misalignment occupy the deepest level of the causal hierarchy. Lack of accountability and governance and data privacy emerge as terminal outcomes. All three analytical methods converge on a conclusion: agentic AI risks originate at the institutional layer, with technical risks acting as transmission mechanisms. Practical implications The findings indicate that effective governance requires that workforce capability, data integrity and objective-function alignment are addressed before deployment. The stratified agentic AI governance framework is proposed that translates hierarchical structure into a sequenced intervention architecture, providing practitioners with governance priorities organized by risk-propagation logic. Originality/value This paper contributes a systematically derived risk taxonomy and a causally weighted governance map for agentic AI risks in supply chains. Five propositions are derived from the causal structure and are advanced as a testable research agenda.

record.abstract_text: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can both enhance and constrain employee creativity, yet the mechanisms underlying these divergent effects remain unclear. This study examines how augmentation and automation motivations for GenAI usage shape employee creativity through distinct knowledge-processing mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on dual-process theory and self-regulation theory, we distinguish augmentation and automation motivations for GenAI usage and propose distinct cognitive mechanisms linking them to creativity. We test the hypotheses using a multi-wave, multi-source field survey and a scenario-based experiment. Findings Augmentation motivation is positively associated with employee creativity through knowledge integration, whereas automation motivation is negatively related to creativity through knowledge dependence. Conscientiousness strengthens the positive indirect effect of augmentation motivation and attenuates the negative indirect effect of automation motivation on employee creativity. Research limitations/implications Augmentation and automation motivations may coexist and vary across tasks and use episodes. Future research could explore these dynamics, examine how other individual differences shape their effects, and assess whether the consequences of GenAI dependence vary across work contexts. Practical implications Organizations should encourage employees to use GenAI to generate and develop ideas rather than replace their own judgment. Training could help employees critically assess AI-generated suggestions and combine them with their own knowledge. Originality/value This research shifts attention from how much employees use GenAI to why they use it. By distinguishing augmentation and automation motivations, it explains when and why GenAI can enhance or constrain employee creativity through distinct knowledge-processing mechanisms.

record.abstract_text: Purpose As artificial intelligence advances and its application scenarios continue to expand, human–artificial intelligence interaction grows increasingly close. While artificial intelligence brings convenience, it also raises concerns that it may weaken users' cognitive autonomy. To investigate this issue. This study aims to explore the composition of AI dependence and its impact on cognitive autonomy and specific aspects of creative performance. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on cognitive evaluation theory and the elaboration likelihood model to construct a dual-pathway model with instrumental dependence and affective dependence as core variables. The model explains the formation mechanisms of the two types of artificial intelligence dependence and their differential effects on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily examines their potential role in the elaboration dimension of creative performance. A two-stage mixed-method design was employed to test the model. Findings Study 1 found that perceived trust mainly had a positive effect on instrumental dependence. Different dimensions of interactivity differentially affected affective dependence and cognitive autonomy. Mediation analysis further confirmed the core mediating role of Dependence. Study 2, a small-sample exploratory experiment, re-tested selected hypotheses and found a possible negative effect of instrumental dependence on the elaboration dimension of creative performance. Research limitations/implications The main theoretical contribution of this study lies in revealing the dual-pathway formation mechanisms of artificial intelligence dependence and the reshaping effects of different types of dependence on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily explores the potential effects of dependence on elaboration performance. Originality/value The dual-pathway dependence model constructed in this study offers practical implications for understanding how long-term use of artificial intelligence affects cognitive autonomy.

record.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how knowledge workers make sense of GenAI-enabled co-production, with particular attention to authorship ambiguity and its implications for competence attribution, self-evaluation and meaningful work. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative approach based on in-depth interviews with 32 knowledge workers who work directly with GenAI tools, combining inductive coding with abductive interpretation. We used the Gioia methodology to analyze participants' reported experiences and interpretations of human–AI collaboration, with sensemaking informing the interpretation of emergent themes and aggregate dimensions. Findings The findings identify authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. When GenAI contributes to ideation, analysis, drafting, coding or other knowledge-intensive outputs, workers may find it difficult to distinguish their own contribution from that of the technology. Participants responded to this ambiguity differently. Some reconstructed their expertise around judgment, validation and contextualization and experienced GenAI as extending their professional capability. Others struggled to internalize successful outputs as evidence of their own competence and reported impostor-like experiences and reduced meaningfulness. The findings suggest that experiences of GenAI-enabled co-production depend on whether workers interpret and reconstruct their contribution. Practical implications Managers in comparable knowledge-intensive settings may consider making human judgment visible, clarifying legitimate uses of GenAI and recognizing contributions beyond output speed and quality. Originality/value This study identifies authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. It shows how uncertainty regarding the respective contributions of the worker and GenAI can complicate competence attribution and initiate sensemaking about professional contribution. By explaining how workers' interpretations of authorship ambiguity are associated with divergent identity and meaning outcomes, including enhanced capability, impostor-like experiences and changing meaningfulness, the study extends research on human–AI collaboration beyond its predominant focus on performance and productivity.

record.abstract_text: Purpose This paper extends Luhmann's concept of programmes – decision premises specifying the conditions under which a system's binary code is operatively assigned – into the domain of algorithmically mediated communication. It conceptualises recommendation systems, ranking algorithms and feedback architectures as ambient cognitive programmes: recursive, probabilistic selectors that perturb the structural coupling between social and psychic systems, and examines the constitutional implications of their opacity and transfunctional reach. Design/methodology/approach The study develops a systemic–cybernetic model grounded in Luhmann's social systems theory and the epistemology of autopoietic cognition, integrating Teubner's theory of societal constitutionalism to address the normative dimensions of algorithmic mediation. Analytical illustrations from Facebook and TikTok contrast two recommendation architectures – affinity-based cascading and behavioural-similarity propagation – to demonstrate how the model applies across distinct platform logics. Findings Algorithmic cognitive programmes operate as meta-programmes that reconfigure multiple forms of social differentiation simultaneously, enacting a binary operational distinction of visibility/invisibility through engagement metrics. Their colonisation of communicative environments – by economic imperatives and, as the analysis argues, by the autonomous logic of technical mediation – becomes a constitutional pathology where its effects cannot be contested or corrected, requiring internal self-limiting mechanisms that render operative selection criteria observable to affected systems. Originality/value The paper advances a novel theoretical category – ambient cognitive programmes – that extends Luhmann's organisational typology by identifying a configuration it does not explicitly address: a purpose programme without a terminal goal state that continuously revises the conditional programmes it governs. It connects this analytical framework to Teubner's societal constitutionalism, proposing constitutional observability as a structural condition for the compatibility between algorithmic regimes and communicative pluralism.

record.abstract_text: Purpose The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into Italian public administration raises a central question: can person-centred human resource management practices turn technology from a source of psychosocial strain into an enabler of continuous improvement? This paper explores how formalized and participatory governance of AI adoption, structured around three Kaizen principles, is associated with employee participation in digital change and with the technostress reported by public employees. Design/methodology/approach A theory-informed qualitative multiple-case study was conducted in five organizational cases, namely Italian public administrations engaged in digital transformation projects funded by the Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza (PNRR). In each organization, a manager–officer dyad (10 participants in total) took part in narrative interviews held between October and November 2025, focused on lived experiences of AI adoption, perceptions of human resource management and professional engagement. Transcripts were analysed through deductive, theory-driven content analysis based on the three Kaizen principles (process orientation, step-by-step improvement and human capital orientation) and on the technostress dimensions, followed by within-case and cross-case comparison. Findings Across 10 participant accounts embedded within five organizational cases, practices consistent with Kaizen were associated, within the accounts, with distinct narrative profiles of technostress and engagement. Accounts reporting all three principles described active co-authorship, professional empowerment and emerging roles; accounts reporting none described persistent techno-anxiety, disengagement and eroding professional identity. Among the creators, techno-insecurity is the one most closely tied to how adoption is governed, and is typically accompanied by techno-anxiety as an affective strain response, while overload, invasion, complexity and uncertainty appear in association with specific operating conditions. Intermediate accounts varied with the missing principle and its hierarchical level. Originality/value This paper develops the joint Kaizen–STS framework as an original analytical lens for AI governance in public administration. It provides qualitative evidence that Kaizen-consistent HR governance is associated with less salient technostress, particularly in the governance-related dimensions emerging from the analysis, and with stronger reported participation, professional agency and more favourable organizational conditions for continuous improvement. The study therefore contributes to organization and human resource management research by proposing the vertical governance gap between managerial design and operational experience as a sensitizing concept and offers public managers a diagnostic framework for PNRR-funded digital transformation across heterogeneous public-sector settings.

record.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
record.abstract_text: Silicon Lifecycle Management (SLM) is essential for ensuring the reliability, security, and performance of modern computing platforms. Conventional SLM approaches rely on off-chip or software-only analytics, which lack on-die interpretability. We present X-OCTANE, an explainable on-chip telemetry-based anomaly notification engine. X–OCTANE is a hybrid explainability framework that integrates Causal-Preserving Mutual Information (CP–MI) with SHAP-based feature attribution for interpretable feature ranking and selection. The proposed feature rank-and-selection procedure retains competitive safety-oriented anomaly detection and bolsters security-specific in-field monitoring of compute platforms. For the 7 nm ASAP technology, X-OCTANE achieves competitive anomaly detection performance with less than 0.50% CPU die area and 1.0% non-idle power overhead. In addition, X–OCTANE improves anomaly-driven diagnosis accuracy by over 7% on average. Experimental validation using the PAMPAR benchmark suite on two separate experimental platforms demonstrates enhanced anomaly detection and diagnosis through the proposed explainable feature-rank-and-selection method. X–OCTANE establishes a scalable and transparent foundation for on-chip SLM analytics, unifying detection fidelity with causal interpretability.

record.abstract_text: Table Question Answering (TableQA) requires reasoning over natural language questions and structured tables and remains challenging due to noisy evidence and complex multi-step reasoning. Recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based approaches typically adopt decomposition–reasoning–validation pipelines that combine Chain-of-Thought (CoT) decomposition, Direct Prompting (DP), Python Agent (PyAgent) execution, and self-validation. However, these methods still largely rely on unconstrained LLM reasoning during decomposition, which may introduce unsupported sub-questions and irrelevant evidence expansion. We propose EV idence- A ware (EVA), a framework that explicitly grounds decomposition on question-relevant table evidence before reasoning begins. EVA first extracts evidence-aware relational structures that associate question semantics with supporting table attributes, thereby constraining sub-question generation within a grounded evidence space. EVA further introduces relation-guided validation and integrates both DP and PyAgent reasoning to improve robustness across different reasoning patterns. Experiments on datasets across multiple LLMs demonstrate that EVA consistently improves reasoning reliability and achieves strong performance across diverse TableQA settings.

record.title: AI-driven approaches for food risk assessment: current advances and future trends

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a tool to support food risk assessment and broader food safety activities in response to the growing complexity of global food supply chains, emerging foodborne hazards, and evolving food fraud practices. Unlike previous reviews that have largely focused on individual AI technologies or specific applications, this review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), transformer-based models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), multimodal learning, and emerging AI paradigms within a unified framework relevant to food risk assessment and food safety decision-making. The review examines their applications in hazard identification, contamination detection, predictive microbiology, risk classification, food fraud detection, surveillance, traceability, and decision-support systems. Particular attention is given to the strengths, limitations, interpretability, validation requirements, and implementation challenges associated with different AI approaches. The integration of AI with multimodal data sources, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, spectroscopy, biosensors, and advanced analytical platforms is also discussed as a means to improve risk prediction, monitoring, and early-warning capabilities. Key challenges include data quality and availability, model generalizability, limited external validation, computational requirements, interpretability, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging developments, including foundation models, federated learning, blockchain, digital twins, edge AI, and multimodal frameworks, are highlighted as promising directions for future research. Overall, this review provides a critical comparative framework for understanding the evolving role of AI in food risk assessment and related food safety applications, while identifying key scientific, technical, and regulatory priorities for future development and implementation. publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

record.abstract_text: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) companions are increasingly used by post-secondary students for emotional support, stress management, and self-management, yet their potential implications for primary care in this population remain unclear. Students may engage with AI companions before encountering purpose-built therapeutic chatbots, which are more often accessed through intentional health-seeking or professional guidance. This distinction may position AI companions as an earlier influence on self-management and subsequent help-seeking. Objective: To examine how artificial intelligence (AI) companions may influence stress regulation, sleep quality, symptom interpretation, and healthcare-seeking behaviour among post-secondary students, and to identify the principal benefits, risks, and unresolved questions relevant to primary care. Methods: A conceptual narrative review was undertaken using literature identified through Harvard University’s Hollis Library and Google Scholar. Evidence related to AI companions, academic stress, sleep quality, emotional support, healthcare-seeking behaviour, primary care, and digital mental health was synthesized using Stress & Coping Theory and the stress-buffering hypothesis as theoretical foundations. Results: AI companions may support stress appraisal, cognitive reframing, emotional reflection, symptom articulation, and self-management before clinical encounters. However, they may also contribute to emotional overreliance, misinformation, reassurance seeking, sleep disruption, and altered help-seeking behaviour. This review proposes conceptual mechanisms linking AI companion engagement with stress regulation, sleep, and pathways into primary care while identifying relational intensity as a clinically meaningful dimension of engagement beyond frequency alone. Conclusion: AI companions should be understood as adjunctive rather than substitutive support. Their clinical relevance is based on how they can shape patients’ experiences before obtaining primary care. Longitudinal research is needed to determine how patterns of engagement influence stress, sleep, and healthcare utilization over time.

record.title: Does Graph Structure Improve AI-Generated Text Detection? A Controlled Audit with Tuned Baselines

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Graph neural network (GNN) detectors of AI-generated text report state-of-the-art accuracy, and the architectural claim that graph topology captures signals invisible to sequential classifiers is now common in the literature. We report the complete lifecycle of one such detector, from construction to falsification. AEGIS, a graph attention network over k-nearest-neighbour text graphs with multi-signal edge weights, reaches 98.50% accuracy on scientific abstracts with only 73K trainable parameters, outperforming five established baselines. We then subject our own system to the evaluation its headline number deserves: generation-time length control, format normalization, leakage-free splits, a tuned frozen-embedding probe as the calibrated null, and a 10 × 10 cross-generator transfer study over three seeds. Under this protocol the graph's apparent contribution collapses from +0.240 AUROC over a surface baseline to −0.0004 AUROC against the tuned probe, inside the measured replication noise floor, and the two detectors' transfer geographies are near-identical (ρ = 0.986). A single untuned regularization default manufactured a +0.027 phantom advantage. The structural differences the graph encodes are real, but they are a re-encoding of information already present in the embeddings. We distil the audit into a practical checklist for evaluating architectural claims in text detection, and argue that accuracy numbers and mechanism claims must be validated separately.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background AI is increasingly embedded in health care and digital health applications, shaping clinical processes as well as how patients access information and participate in care. Research on bias in medical AI has largely focused on technical and performance-related disparities. Less attention has been paid to how such biases may affect patients’ access, understanding, trust, and opportunities for meaningful involvement in care. Objective This scoping review aimed to map how studies of bias in medical AI describe patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment and the digital divide and to identify gaps across technical, social, structural, and patient-centered perspectives. Methods This scoping review followed JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute) methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost databases were searched in August 2025 and supplemented by Google Scholar searches. Peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 onward were included if they addressed bias in medical AI and described patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment or digital inequality. Data charting focused on AI application types, bias dimensions, patient empowerment domains, digital divide–related factors, intersectionality, and debiasing strategies. Findings were synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results The search identified 497 records, of which 22 studies met the inclusion criteria. Bias was represented as a multidimensional sociotechnical phenomenon, with social bias identified most frequently (21/22 studies), followed by algorithmic bias (16/22 studies), structural bias (14/22 studies), and design-related bias (12/22 studies). Patient empowerment was most frequently addressed through involvement in care (n=13), followed by health literacy (n=9) and trust and assurance (n=7), whereas broader psychosocial and everyday-life domains were addressed less frequently. Digital divide–related factors were identified in 19 of the 22 studies, with digital literacy and usability barriers reported most frequently. Seven studies considered 2 or more social or structural dimensions of disadvantage. Although many studies discussed approaches that could mitigate bias-related barriers, explicit empirical evaluation of debiasing strategies in relation to patient empowerment or digital equity was largely absent. Conclusions Patient-related consequences of bias in medical AI extend beyond algorithmic performance and are reflected in access, understanding, trust, and involvement in care. Broader empowerment dimensions, multidimensional disadvantage, and empirically evaluated mitigation strategies remain comparatively underexplored.

record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. At the same time, less consistent effects for behavioral regulation point to an important design challenge: supporting learners in knowing what to do and why to do it does not necessarily ensure that they will translate those intentions into effective action. Grounded in Winne and Hadwin's COPES architecture, this conceptual paper tackles a core dilemma in educational technology: how can AI assist learners without eroding the cognitive agency and productive struggle essential to self-regulation? Agustin introduces "productive metacognitive friction" -the deliberate structuring of challenge and discrepancy within AI interaction -as a design mechanism to prevent passive reliance. The article presents five relational design principles alongside an evaluation framework prioritizing learner autonomy, interpretability, process integrity, and long-term developmental growth across both formal education and workplace reskilling environments.Moving from meta-analytic synthesis and conceptual frameworks to empirical classroom research, Gu et al.'s Fostering feedback literacy by scaffolding self-regulated feedback: a comparative study of GenAI and human peers examines the operational mechanisms through which GenAI fosters feedback literacya key component of self-regulated learning. In a comparative mixed-methods study of first-year undergraduates in Hong Kong, the authors compare the developmental impact of GenAI-generated feedback against traditional human peer review. Their findings demonstrate that GenAI yields a statistically significant improvement in feedback literacy over human peer feedback alone. Qualitative evidence reveals that this advantage stems from GenAI's ability to scaffold distinct self-regulatory behaviors: providing immediate, non-judgmental spaces for goal setting, structured planning, critical evaluation, and real-time self-reflection. By removing the interpersonal friction and psychological safety concerns common in peer review, GenAI emerges as an effective tool for cultivating student feedback literacy.Finally, Chang et al.'s "Should I tell my teacher?" Their findings illuminate a key tension: while transparent disclosure to instructors correlates with proactive self-regulated learning behaviors (a "transparent-disclosure pattern"), fear of academic judgment and social stigmatization often triggers an "anxious-concealment pattern." Research and design must examine how AI can scaffold regulatory processes, support learner autonomy and human agency, and safeguard against cognitive over-reliance.

record.venue: Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics
record.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded across the scientific research lifecycle, while prevailing governance remains centered on disclosure of tool use and the assignment of responsibility to human authors. We argue that disclosure is necessary but insufficient because it does not establish that researchers understood, verified, challenged, and authorized the AI-assisted processes that shaped scientific claims. We define this disconnect as the epistemic accountability gap and develop the Lifecycle Epistemic Accountability Framework (LEAF) as a testable theory of how meaningful human control can be preserved across AI-assisted knowledge production. Drawing on a structured integrative review and critical interpretive synthesis, LEAF links four human-control capacities—competence, contestability, intervention authority, and traceable ownership—supported by evaluability by design, to five lifecycle checkpoints spanning evidence identification, study design and ethics, data processing and analysis, interpretation, and reporting or knowledge translation. The framework proposes that accountability improves when oversight is exercised prospectively at epistemically consequential decision points, documented through an audit trail, and calibrated to epistemic materiality: the extent to which AI assistance can alter the validity, interpretation, or consequences of a scientific claim. Six propositions specify testable relationships among disclosure, epistemic materiality, meaningful human control, lifecycle checkpoints, auditability, and defensibility of scientific claims. LEAF therefore shifts AI research governance from retrospective visibility to prospective, risk-proportionate control. We identify boundary conditions, implementation pathways, and an empirical research agenda for testing the framework across disciplines and resource settings. LEAF's distinctive explanatory mechanism is conditional: epistemic materiality escalates oversight, evaluability enables four human capacities, lifecycle checkpoints interrupt error propagation, and retained audit evidence makes consequential decisions answerable.

Following the Analysis and Design phases of the ADDIE research-and-development approach, we synthesised recent experimental, meta-analytic, and survey evidence to derive design requirements, translated them into a stage-by-stage instructional specification, built a process-sensitive assessment rubric, and defined a quasi-experimental and qualitative validation plan for Indonesian higher education. The results are the model and its components: an evidence-to-design mapping, the FAVIC stage specification, a three-level process-sensitive rubric, and an evaluation design with hypotheses. Conclusion: SC-AIM offers lecturers a concrete, theory-grounded sequence that places human reasoning before and after AI assistance and makes verification an assessed activity, giving higher education a ready-to-use pedagogical model for developing analytical and logical reasoning in the age of generative AI.

record.abstract_text: This research aimed to assess awareness of generative AI limitations, highlight its advantages, and identify potential threats from misuse, focusing on differences in opinions between future educators and students from non-education fields. The data were collected through surveying 931 undergraduate students of a private university in the Philippines. The researchers used a comparative-correlational research design with a qualitative strand. The study found moderate awareness of generative AI’s limitations (M = 3.31, SD = 0.94) and a moderate-to-cautious attitude toward its implementation (M = 3.15, SD = 0.87). Education students showed higher awareness than students from other majors (d = 0.40), while differences in usage, perception, and fear of skills deteriorating were negligible (d = 0.14–0.25) and, to some extent, neutralized in robustness checks. Differences between genders and years of study in perceptions were minor. The findings suggest that future teachers’ curricula should include a course on AI literacy and emphasize developing critical thinking skills to prepare students for implementing generative AI solutions in teaching practices.

record.abstract_text: The study aimed to check the association of ChatGPT use and critical thinking on academic integrity. The research design is cross-sectional correlational study to collect data from university students aged from 18 to 23 years old. The sample size was 600 students taken via purposive sampling from the University of Gujrat, Pakistan. Standardized psychological scales of ChatGPT usage scale, critical thinking evaluation scale, and academic integrity scales were used. Our findings showed that ChatGPT has no significant effect on academic integrity but has positive effect on critical thinking. While critical thinking has positive effect on academic integrity. It showed that ChatGPT doesn’t directly change cheating behavior, but it can boost critical thinking for students, and that improved critical thinking is what increases academic integrity. Implications of the findings are discussed.

record.abstract_text: Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have emerged as powerful paradigms in artificial intelligence, enabling systems to learn patterns from data and automate complex decision-making processes. This paper presents a comprehensive review of machine learning and deep learning approaches, focusing on their fundamental principles, commonly used techniques, and diverse real-world applications. The study discusses core ML algorithms, neural network architectures, and the role of deep learning models in solving complex problems such as image recognition, natural language processing, healthcare analytics, and recommendation systems. Furthermore, the paper highlights the key differences between traditional machine learning methods and deep learning models, emphasizing their strengths and limitations. Recent research trends, including explainable AI, transfer learning, and large-scale data-driven modeling, are also examined to provide insights into the evolving landscape of intelligent systems. By synthesizing findings from recent literature, this review aims to offer researchers and practitioners a clearer understanding of current developments and future opportunities in machine learning and deep learning technologies.

record.title: Neural Mechanisms of Willed Attention Control

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Cueing paradigms are commonly used to study the neural mechanisms of visual spatial attention control. In these paradigms, each trial starts with an external cue, which instructs the subject to pay covert attention to a spatial location in anticipation of an impending stimulus (instructed attention). Recent work has introduced a new type of cue which prompts the subject to spontaneously decide which spatial location to attend (willed attention). We studied the neural mechanisms of willed attention control by analyzing fMRI and EEG data recorded at two institutions (UF and UC Davis) using the same willed attention paradigm. The findings include: (1) both instructional cues and the choice cue activated the DAN, (2) the choice cue additionally activated a frontoparietal decision network consisting of dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), anterior insula (AI), anterior prefrontal cortex (APFC), dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), and inferior parietal lobule (IPL), (3) the decision about where to attend can be decoded in frontoparietal decision network in choice trials but not in instructional trials, and (4) EEG alpha oscillation patterns immediately preceding the choice cue, but not the instructional cues, predicted the postcue direction of attention and the frontoparietal decision network activity. Based on these findings we proposed a model of willed attention control suggesting how the direction of visual spatial attention was decided upon in the absence of external instructions.
